Unifying Dirac Spin Liquids on Square and
Shastry–Sutherland Lattices via Fermionic Deconfined Criticality

Andreas Feuerpfeil 1,2,⋆\star, Leyna Shackleton 3, Atanu Maity 1, Ronny Thomale 1,4, Subir Sachdev 5,2 and Yasir Iqbal 4,†\dagger

1Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik and Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, Universität Würzburg, 97074 Würzburg, Germany

2Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA

3Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139, USA

4Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India

5Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA 02138, USA

⋆\star andreas.feuerpfeil@uni-wuerzburg.de , †\dagger yiqbal@physics.iitm.ac.in

Abstract

We present a fermionic gauge theory for deconfined quantum criticality on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice and reveal its shared low-energy field-theoretic structure with the square lattice. Starting from an 𝐒𝐔⁡(𝟐)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux parent state, we construct a continuum theory of Dirac spinons coupled to an 𝐒𝐔⁡(𝟐)\mathrm{SU}(2) gauge field and adjoint Higgs fields whose condensates drive transitions to a staggered-flux 𝐔⁡(𝟏)\mathrm{U}(1) spin liquid and a gapless Z𝟐\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid. While the Shastry–Sutherland lattice permits additional symmetry-allowed fermion bilinears compared to the square lattice, the quantum field theories are identical up to additional irrelevant terms. Consequently, the Higgs potential structure and the leading low-energy theory coincide with the square-lattice case at the quantum critical point. The 𝐒𝐎⁡(𝟓)\mathrm{SO}(5) critical point is expected to realize conformal deconfined criticality: we analyze it in a large-flavor expansion, calculate its critical exponents, and identify the Yukawa coupling between the fermions and Higgs fields as the relevant perturbation that destabilizes it, consistent with pseudocritical behavior observed in recent Monte Carlo studies. We show that the emergent 𝐒𝐎⁡(𝟓)\mathrm{SO}(5) order parameter acquires a large anomalous dimension at the critical point, leading to strongly enhanced Néel and VBS susceptibilities—a hallmark of fermionic deconfined quantum criticality consistent with numerical studies. Our results place recent numerical evidence for a gapless Z𝟐\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice within a controlled field-theoretic framework and demonstrate that fermionic deconfined criticality on the square lattice—including critical exponents and stability—extends to frustrated lattices with reduced symmetry.

Quantum phase transitions in two-dimensional antiferromagnets can fall outside the conventional Landau–Ginzburg–Wilson paradigm when the critical degrees of freedom are fractionalized and coupled to emergent gauge fields. A prominent example is deconfined criticality, where continuous transitions can occur between phases with distinct broken symmetries, such as Néel order and valence-bond-solid (VBS) order [50, 47, 46]. Considerable insight into such transitions has been obtained by formulating effective field theories of Dirac fermions coupled to gauge fields; this framework provides a unified description of magnetically ordered phases, spin liquids, and their proximate critical points [22, 28, 54].

Within this fermionic framework, SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) gauge theories of Dirac spinons play a central role [2]. In these theories, adjoint Higgs fields reduce the gauge symmetry to U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) or Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}, yielding staggered-flux [28] and gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin-liquid phases [66, 21, 23], respectively. On the square lattice, such Higgs theories [42, 43] have been shown to capture deconfined critical points separating Néel order, VBS order, and gapless spin liquids, with the structure of the low-energy theory strongly constrained by lattice symmetries and their projective symmetry group (PSG) realizations [58, 49, 59].

The Shastry–Sutherland lattice provides a natural setting in which to examine these ideas beyond the square lattice. While retaining nontrivial point-group symmetries, it breaks several lattice symmetries of the square lattice and supports additional frustration through diagonal couplings [56]. Recently, numerical [68, 62, 60, 27, 13, 9] and variational studies [32] by some of us have provided evidence for a gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid stabilized in the spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg model on this lattice, denoted Z3000; it can be interpreted as a descendant of a staggered-flux U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state [28] and, ultimately, of an SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux parent state originally proposed by Affleck and Marston for square-lattice antiferromagnets [2, 3, 15, 64, 66].

A central issue in extending fermionic deconfined criticality to the Shastry–Sutherland lattice is the role of reduced lattice symmetry. Whereas it might help to microscopically stabilize quantum paramagnets from the viewpoint of ground state energy density through enhanced tuning of frustration, it also enormously broadens the scope of symmetry-allowed ground state candidates: implementing the relevant PSG requires an enlarged 2×22\times 2 unit cell, which reorganizes the Dirac fermions and their symmetry transformations. While the square-lattice �\pi-flux theory features Dirac valleys protected at distinct momenta, this protection is lifted in the Shastry–Sutherland embedding once lattice-specific perturbations are included. Furthermore, the reduced space-group symmetry enlarges the set of symmetry-allowed Yukawa couplings between fermion bilinears and Higgs fields, raising the question of whether the resulting continuum theory retains the same structure as in the square-lattice case. We show that while the reduced symmetry of the Shastry–Sutherland lattice allows for additional symmetry-allowed Yukawa couplings between Dirac fermions and Higgs fields, all such couplings share the same scaling dimension at leading order in a controlled large-NN expansion. Consequently, within this framework, lattice frustration does not modify the stability properties of the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) critical point relative to the square-lattice theory.

The main results of this work are as follows. We construct a fermionic-spinon field theory for the Shastry–Sutherland model starting from the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux parent state and derive the continuum perturbations that generate the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) staggered-flux and Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin-liquid descendants. The resulting continuum description is a Dirac theory coupled to an SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) gauge field and three real adjoint Higgs fields, whose condensates encode the Higgs transitions between these phases. At the level of the most relevant couplings controlling the Higgs transitions, the resulting Majorana–Higgs theory coincides with the corresponding square-lattice theory, including a global SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry [59, 11]. The reduced symmetry of the Shastry–Sutherland lattice permits additional fermion bilinears and gradient terms, but these do not change the scaling dimensions or appear only as symmetry-allowed subleading perturbations. We further determine the most general Higgs potential consistent with the microscopic symmetries and show that its structure is identical to the square-lattice case to all orders, implying the same mean-field Higgs phase structure underlying the sequence Néel →\rightarrow Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid →\rightarrow VBS. Finally, we extract consequences for the competing Néel and VBS channels, including characteristic low-energy corrections to their susceptibilities.

In previous analyses for the square lattice [52, 51], it was assumed that the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) breaking perturbations were strongly relevant, and this led to consideration of a critical theory without SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5), or even Lorentz, symmetry. The present paper will take a complementary point of view, assuming that the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) breaking perturbations are at best weakly relevant. We will focus on a theory with exact SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry, an SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) gauge field, Nf=2N_{f}=2 massless, fundamental Dirac fermions and Nb=2N_{b}=2 adjoint Higgs fields. Studies of the Néel–VBS transition on the square lattice are described by Nf=2N_{f}=2, Nb=0N_{b}=0: state-of-the-art Monte Carlo studies increasingly indicate that this SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) point is pseudocritical or multifractal rather than truly conformal [35, 61, 63, 71, 7, 6, 57], suggesting a wide pre-asymptotic regime with approximate SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry [53, 71]. These results strongly imply the existence of a conformal fixed point with exact SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry for the Nf=2N_{f}=2, Nb=2N_{b}=2 case, as the additional critical Higgs fields can only enhance the stability of the CFT. We will study this CFT in the large-Nf,bN_{f,b} expansion, and compute scaling dimensions of various observables.

Turning to the onset of the gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid, we consider the perturbative influence of the Yukawa couplings which break both SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) and Lorentz symmetry present for this case (for both the square and Shastry–Sutherland lattices) at the fixed point with exact SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry. While our renormalization-group analysis of the associated gauge theory finds the leading SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-breaking perturbation to be relevant at large NN, and hence to destabilize the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-symmetric fixed point at the lowest energies, this does not contradict either earlier field-theoretic expectations or recent numerical work. First, the large-NN expansion does not control the fixed point at physical, finite NN in strongly coupled gauge theories, but rather correctly identifies the operator content [44]. Second, a defining and quantitatively testable signature of such fermionic deconfined critical points is the appearance of unusually large anomalous dimensions for the competing Néel and VBS order parameters. These have been observed numerically in JJ–QQ models and related systems, and sharply distinguish deconfined criticality from conventional O⁡(3)\mathrm{O}(3) universality classes. In this work, we compute these anomalous dimensions analytically for the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux theory relevant to both square and Shastry–Sutherland lattices. Taken together, these results suggest that while the gapless Dirac spinon theory on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice is ultimately unstable at the lowest energies, it can remain a valid and predictive description over an extended low-energy window, which may be relevant for experimentally accessible regimes.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Sec. 1 we introduce the fermionic spinon formulation and the Z3000 Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin-liquid ansatz on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice. Section 2 derives the continuum SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux theory and the Higgs perturbations leading to the U800 and Z3000 states, and presents the resulting Majorana–Higgs Lagrangian and Higgs potential, together with a classification of all symmetry-allowed fermion bilinears up to first order in gradients under the Shastry–Sutherland space group. Section 3 presents a renormalization-group analysis of the resulting gauge theory including a calculation of the critical exponents, and Sec. 4 discusses the implications for deconfined criticality in frustrated quantum magnets.

1 Gapless 𝒁𝟐\bm{\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}} spin liquid on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice

The Shastry–Sutherland Hamiltonian for a spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet is defined on the lattice, see Fig. 1, as

H^=Js​∑⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩square𝐒^𝒊⋅𝐒^𝒋+Jd​∑⟨𝒊,𝒋⟩dimer𝐒^𝒊⋅𝐒^𝒋.\hat{H}=J_{s}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}}\rangle_{\mathrm{square}}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{\bm{i}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{\bm{j}}+J_{d}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}}\rangle_{\mathrm{dimer}}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{\bm{i}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{\bm{j}}\,. (1)

where 𝐒^𝒊\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{\bm{i}} denotes the spin operator at site 𝒊{\bm{i}}, and JsJ_{s} and JdJ_{d} are the exchange couplings on the edges of the squares and on the dimer bonds, respectively (see Fig. 1(b)). Equation (1) accurately models the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} Shastry–Sutherland compound SrCu2(BO3)2, which realizes an exact dimer-singlet ground state at ambient pressure [25]. Hydrostatic pressure tunes the effective ratio Jd/JsJ_{d}/J_{s}, driving a sequence of quantum phase transitions resolved by thermodynamic, spectroscopic, and neutron-scattering experiments, including an intermediate gapped plaquette phase followed by antiferromagnetic order [19, 69]. In the fermionic gauge-theory framework, increasing Jd/JsJ_{d}/J_{s} corresponds to Higgs-induced reductions of the emergent SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) gauge structure, whose confined descendants naturally account for plaquette and Néel phases, providing a materials setting for pressure-driven deconfined or pseudocritical behavior [14, 18].

We therefore formulate the fermionic spinon theory for Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids [65] on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice. We begin by reexpressing the spin operators with respect to spinons f𝒊​�,�=↑,↓f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha},\alpha=\uparrow,\downarrow for sites 𝒊=(ix,iy){\bm{i}}=(i_{x},i_{y}) [1]:

Following Wen [66], we introduce a Nambu spinor

𝒊=(f𝒊↑f𝒊↓†),{}_{{\bm{i}}}=\begin{pmatrix}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}\,, (3)

which leads to the Bogoliubov Hamiltonian

2 Continuum theory for Higgs transition from 𝐒𝐔⁡(𝟐)\bm{\mathrm{SU}(2)} to 𝒁𝟐\bm{\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}}

2.1 𝐒𝐔⁡(𝟐)\bm{\mathrm{SU}(2)} �\bm{\pi}-flux state

We begin by working out the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) gauge theory based on the PSG ansatz for the �\pi-flux state [2, 66]. We replace the Nambu spinor by a matrix operator of Majorana fermions

ℱ𝒊=(f𝒊↑−f𝒊↓†f𝒊↓f𝒊↑†).\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}=\begin{pmatrix}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}&&-f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}&&f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}\,. (18)

This ansatz respects the square lattice symmetries and is, up to a gauge transformation, identical to the ansatz studied in Ref. [52]. To study the low-energy physics, we express the Hamiltonian in momentum space

where the summation over mx,mym_{x},m_{y} is implicit. The Hamiltonian features a Dirac point at �=(0,0)\Gamma=(0,0) with a four-fold degeneracy arising from the sublattice degrees of freedom. The dispersion of the U800 spin liquid is shown in Fig. 10, where '=�\varphi=\pi corresponds to the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux state.

In comparison, on the square lattice, introducing the sublattice degree of freedom mxm_{x} is sufficient to restore translational invariance of the ansatz. This yields two Dirac points associated with a valley degree of freedom v=0,1v=0,1 at kx=0k_{x}=0 and ky=0,�k_{y}=0,\pi. These points are back-folded to the �\Gamma point due to the doubling of the unit cell in the yy-direction. To make the valley degree of freedom explicit, we introduce two low-energy, two-component fermions 𝒳𝒓,mx,v{\mathcal{X}}_{{\bm{r}},m_{x},v}:

ℱ𝒓,mx,my=∑mx′�mx,mx′x​𝒳𝒓,mx′,0+�my,myz​𝒳𝒓,mx,1.\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{r}},m_{x},m_{y}}=\sum_{m_{x}^{\prime}}\rho^{x}_{m_{x},m_{x}^{\prime}}{\mathcal{X}}_{{\bm{r}},m_{x}^{\prime},0}+\kappa^{z}_{m_{y},m_{y}}{\mathcal{X}}_{{\bm{r}},m_{x},1}\,. (26)

Since Eq. (26) only rewrites ℱ\mathcal{F} as a linear combination of low-energy modes in the sublattice/valley sector, with real coefficients given by �x\rho^{x} and �z\kappa^{z}, the Majorana reality condition

We introduce the Pauli matrices �a\mu^{a} acting on the valley degree of freedom. However, this protection is eventually lifted by perturbations due to backfolding effects in the Shastry–Sutherland model. 𝒳→𝒳​L,{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{X}}L\,, (31)

for which the reality condition implies

where �a​b​c\epsilon_{abc} is the Levi-Civita symbol. These terms are again identical to the square lattice case [52] and lead to a mean-field phase diagram with three different phases as exemplified in Fig. 2.

In the following, we prove that the symmetry-allowed terms in the Higgs potential are identical for any lattice whose symmetry group is a superset of the Shastry–Sutherland wallpaper group p4g and a subset of the square lattice wallpaper group p4mm. To this end, we demonstrate that any term allowed on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice is also symmetry-allowed on the square lattice.

Due to invariance under 𝒯\mathcal{T}, any such term is invariant under PxP_{x} and PyP_{y}, and the presence of GxG_{x} implies invariance under TyT_{y} (see Tab. 1). As we can represent the remaining generators as Tx=Py∘GxT_{x}=P_{y}\circ G_{x} and R�/2=Px∘�x​yR_{\pi/2}=P_{x}\circ\sigma_{xy}, it is also invariant under TxT_{x} and R�/2R_{\pi/2}. Therefore, any symmetry-allowed term on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice automatically satisfies square lattice symmetry, and the structure of the Higgs potential is thus identical to arbitrary order.

As has been previously argued on the square lattice [55], there exists a trivial monopole for the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) staggered flux state [4], which proliferates and is expected to break the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) spin liquid down to either Néel or VBS order [54, 52]. As the Shastry–Sutherland symmetry group is a subset of the one of the square lattice, this monopole still transforms trivially under the Shastry–Sutherland symmetry group and PSG, so we expect the same instability towards Néel and VBS order.

Similarly, we expect the fate of the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux state to lead to Néel or one of the columnar or plaquette VBS orders [61]. A large-NfN_{f} analysis of the �\pi-flux to Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid transition [52] finds enhanced Néel correlations at the critical point, suggesting that the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux state may prefer to confine to Néel order, whilst the U800 spin liquid confines to a VBS state. However, we stress that the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux theory on its own has no preference to either phase, and that different points in the phase diagram even in the same spin liquid phase could lead to different confined phases depending on microscopic details. Therefore, it is possible that some parts of the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) spin-liquid phase confine to columnar VBS order, whilst others confine to plaquette VBS order as observed numerically [46, 40, 12, 67, 29, 30, 32, 39].

2.5 Symmetry-allowed couplings

In the form of Eq. (46), by ignoring the gradient terms, which have a larger scaling dimension and are thus less relevant, the critical theory is identical to the square lattice case [52]. As the mean-field ansatz on the lattice might lack terms that are symmetry-allowed in the continuum theory, we now analyze all allowed fermion bilinears that respect time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}, which acts as 𝒯=i​�y​K\mathcal{T}=i\sigma^{y}K, as well as lattice symmetries. Time-reversal symmetry is implemented identically on both the square and Shastry–Sutherland lattice. For the SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux state and U800 up to nearest-neighbor hopping, their PSG is consistent with the square lattice symmetries defined as

Tx:(ix,iy)↦(ix+1,iy),Ty:(ix,iy)↦(ix,iy+1),Px:(ix,iy)↦(−ix,iy),Py:(ix,iy)↦(ix,−iy),R�/2:(ix,iy)↦(−iy,ix).\begin{split}T_{x}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(i_{x}+1,i_{y})\,,\\ T_{y}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(i_{x},i_{y}+1)\,,\\ P_{x}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(-i_{x},i_{y})\,,\\ P_{y}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(i_{x},-i_{y})\,,\\ R_{\pi/2}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(-i_{y},i_{x})\,.\end{split} (48)

The square lattice symmetry is explicitly broken for the Z3000 ansatz, which only preserves the Shastry–Sutherland symmetry group p​4​gp4g as depicted in Fig. 1(a):

T2​x:(ix,iy)↦(ix+2,iy),T2​y:(ix,iy)↦(ix,iy+2),Gx:(ix,iy)↦(ix+1,−iy),Gy:(ix,iy)↦(−ix,iy+1),�x​y:(ix,iy)↦(iy,ix),�x​y¯:(ix,iy)↦(−iy+1,−ix+1),C4:(ix,iy)↦(−iy+2,ix−1).\begin{split}T_{2x}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(i_{x}+2,i_{y})\,,\\ T_{2y}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(i_{x},i_{y}+2)\,,\\ G_{x}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(i_{x}+1,-i_{y})\,,\\ G_{y}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(-i_{x},i_{y}+1)\,,\\ \sigma_{xy}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(i_{y},i_{x})\,,\\ \sigma_{x\bar{y}}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(-i_{y}+1,-i_{x}+1)\,,\\ C_{4}:(i_{x},i_{y})&\mapsto(-i_{y}+2,i_{x}-1)\,.\end{split} (49)

The projective action for the relevant spin liquids is defined in Appendix A. For simplicity, we set all global SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) matrices to the identity.

3 Renormalization study of the critical 𝐒𝐔⁡(𝟐)\bm{\mathrm{SU}(2)} gauge theory

The stability of the emergent SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry at the deconfined quantum critical point remains a subject of active debate. While the fermionic SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux theory exhibits an enlarged SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry that unifies the Néel and valence-bond-solid order parameters [47, 50, 35, 61], a growing body of analytical and numerical work indicates that this fixed point is generically unstable in the strict infrared due to symmetry-allowed perturbations, most notably the Yukawa coupling between Dirac spinons and Higgs fields [61, 63, 70]. Importantly, this instability does not preclude the appearance of robust SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-symmetric scaling over extended intermediate length scales. Instead, it is now widely understood that the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) fixed point acts as a pseudocritical or “walking” fixed point, controlling a broad pre-asymptotic regime before renormalization-group flows ultimately run away at the lowest energies [53, 34, 71, 57]. This picture reconciles large-NN field-theoretic analyses with state-of-the-art Monte Carlo simulations, which consistently observe approximate SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry, emergent operator degeneracies, and universal scaling over many decades despite an eventual departure from true conformality. In this sense, the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) theory provides the appropriate organizing framework for both the square-lattice and Shastry–Sutherland antiferromagnets, even though it does not represent a stable infrared fixed point. To assess the ultimate fate of this fixed point, we reformulate the theory in terms of Nf=2N_{f}=2 flavors of complex Dirac fermions, generalizing the model to include v=1,…,Nfv=1,\dots,N_{f} valleys and a Higgs flavor index �=1,…,Nb/2\alpha=1,\dots,N_{b}/2 to facilitate a controlled expansion.

The Dirac fermions can be expressed with respect to the Majorana matrix operator as

The first two components correspond to the VBS order, whilst the last three correspond to the Néel order. We begin by expressing the VBS order parameter with respect to the Dirac fermions in Eq. (53):

for the physically relevant values Nf=Nb=2N_{f}=N_{b}=2.

The exponent is negative, so the susceptibility diverges as k→0k\to 0, but only weakly, a consequence of the large anomalous dimension �\eta associated with deconfined quantum criticality [47]. In real space, the susceptibility follows the dual scaling:

Such large anomalous dimensions are a hallmark of fermionic deconfined quantum criticality and reflect the fractionalized nature of the critical degrees of freedom.

Large anomalous dimensions have also been reported in numerical studies of JJ–QQ models, which find �≈0.3\eta\approx 0.3–0.350.35 for the Néel–VBS order parameter [5]. The common feature, an anomalous dimension far above that of the O⁡(3)\mathrm{O}(3) class, supports the interpretation of both systems as exhibiting pseudocritical SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-symmetric behavior governed by fractionalized degrees of freedom.

3.5 Renormalization of the Yukawa coupling

Finally, we investigate the stability of the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) critical point by calculating the vertex corrections to the scaling dimension of the Yukawa coupling yy, which breaks both the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry and Lorentz invariance. To this end, we couple the Yukawa terms to a source field and evaluate the vertex corrections mediated by the gauge field. The contributing diagrams are depicted in Fig. 8. Notably, the first diagram contributes twice due to the specific coupling between the Dirac fermions and the boson.

Our objective is to determine the scaling dimensions of the Yukawa coupling for different matrices XsX^{s} acting on the Dirac and valley degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we aim to assess the relative relevance of other symmetry-allowed zeroth-order bilinears that transform as spin singlets (tabulated in Tab. 2 and Tab. 3). We restrict our attention to spin singlets because terms transforming as vectors cannot form a symmetric spin liquid [59]. Consequently, we consider a generic Yukawa coupling to a Higgs field �\Phi of the form

y∑���a ¯v�aXv.y\sum_{\alpha}\Phi_{\alpha}^{a}\bar{\psi}_{v}\tau^{a}X{}_{v}\,. (94)

which yields the scaling dimension for the coupling constant:

We observe that the fluctuations of the Lagrange multiplier act to reduce the scaling dimension of yy (the second term on the right hand side of Eq. (100)), while the gauge field fluctuations act to increase the scaling dimension of yy (the third term on the right hand side of Eq. (100)). This is to be contrasted with the result for the critical exponent �\nu in Eq. (93), where both types of fluctuations decrease the value of �\nu. The large-flavor expansion is not expected to be a reliable estimate of the relative strength of the opposing tendencies in the renormalization of yy, and so the ultimate fate of yy at the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) fixed point remains unclear. Evaluating Eq. (100) directly for the physically relevant Nf=2,Nb=2N_{f}=2,N_{b}=2 yields dim[y(a)]≈1.378>0\dim[y^{(a)}]\approx 1.378>0 and dim[y(b)]≈1.198\dim[y^{(b)}]\approx 1.198. The observation that the Yukawa coupling is more relevant when coupling to the Dirac indices aligns with the findings in Ref. [17].

Applying this to the Shastry–Sutherland lattice discussed in Sec. 2.5.2, the Yukawa couplings Xs=(�z,x�x)yX^{s}=(\mu^{z}{}^{x},\mu^{x}{}^{y}) for the two Higgs fields �1,2\Phi_{1,2}—along with the additional symmetry-allowed terms �xx\mu^{x}{}^{x} and �zy\mu^{z}{}^{y}—all fall under case (a). Consequently, they share the maximum scaling dimension dim[y]=dim[y(a)]≈1.378\dim[y]=\dim[y^{(a)}]\approx 1.378. These are the most relevant Yukawa couplings, demonstrating that the extra symmetry-allowed terms on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice do not alter the scaling dimension compared to the square lattice. Yukawa couplings with other zeroth-order bilinears, corresponding to U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) and Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids other than the ones considered here, possess either an identical or smaller scaling dimension; therefore, within the large-Nf,bN_{f,b} framework, they are not expected to change the ultimate fate of the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) critical point.

The relevance of the Yukawa coupling in the large-NN analysis implies that the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-symmetric fixed point is ultimately unstable in the strict infrared [71] and the relevant quantum field theory is the one studied in [52]. However, extensive numerical studies of deconfined criticality have demonstrated that weakly relevant perturbations can generate an extended regime of approximate SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry and scaling [7, 10], giving rise to pseudocritical or “walking” behavior [35, 53, 34]. In this regime, renormalization-group flows remain close to the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-symmetric fixed point over many decades before eventually running away, leading to apparent universal scaling with well-defined effective critical exponents [57]. From this perspective, the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) fixed point acts as a controlling multicritical structure rather than a true infrared limit, reconciling the large-NN instability with numerical and experimental observations of robust deconfined-like behavior at intermediate scales [61, 24, 20, 16, 36, 30].

4 Conclusion and Discussion

In this work, we have established a unified fermionic gauge-theory description of deconfined criticality on the square and Shastry–Sutherland lattices, demonstrating that their low-energy continuum theories coincide at the level of the most relevant couplings controlling Higgs transitions out of an SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux parent state. Despite the reduced lattice symmetry of the Shastry–Sutherland geometry and the correspondingly enlarged set of symmetry-allowed fermion bilinears, we have shown that all such additional couplings are either irrelevant or share identical scaling dimensions with their square-lattice counterparts within a controlled large-NN expansion. As a result, the structure of the Higgs potential, the emergent SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry unifying Néel and valence-bond-solid order, and the leading operator content at criticality are preserved.

We have also proposed a candidate conformal field theory with SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry: an SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) gauge theory with Nf=2N_{f}=2 massless, fundamental Dirac fermions, and Nb=2N_{b}=2, critical adjoint Higgs scalars. The Nf=2N_{f}=2, Nb=0N_{b}=0 case has been extensively studied earlier, with evidence for pseudocritical behavior [35, 61, 63, 71, 7, 6, 57]. Adding Nb=2N_{b}=2 adjoint Higgs scalars can reasonably be expected to stabilize the theory to a true conformal theory. This theory is proposed to control the physics near the boundary between the Néel and gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid states.

Our renormalization-group analysis identifies the Yukawa coupling between Dirac spinons and Higgs fields as the leading SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-breaking perturbation, rendering the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-symmetric fixed point unstable at the lowest energies. This instability may nevertheless be compatible with the growing body of numerical evidence indicating pseudocritical or “walking” behavior characterized by approximate SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) symmetry over an extended intermediate regime. Our results suggest that large anomalous dimensions of Néel and VBS order parameters may serve as a robust and experimentally relevant diagnostic of fermionic deconfined criticality, even when the ultimate infrared fixed point is unstable. This reinforces the view of the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) theory as an organizing principle controlling extended pseudocritical regimes in frustrated quantum magnets. Taken together, our results place recent numerical observations of a gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid on the Shastry–Sutherland lattice within a coherent and controlled field-theoretic framework, and demonstrate that fermionic deconfined criticality extends beyond the square lattice to frustrated geometries with reduced symmetry.

Several directions emerge naturally from our analysis. First, while the present work establishes the operator content and leading instabilities of the SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5) critical theory, a quantitative characterization of the associated pseudocritical regime—including crossover scales, finite-size scaling forms, and multifractal operator spectra—would provide a direct bridge to recent large-scale Monte Carlo studies. In this context, it would be particularly interesting to examine whether lattice-specific perturbations can parametrically enhance the extent of the walking regime on frustrated lattices relative to the square lattice.

Second, our framework can be generalized to incorporate additional symmetry-allowed perturbations such as Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions, further-neighbor exchanges, or explicit breaking of spin-rotation symmetry, which are generically present in material realizations of the Shastry–Sutherland lattice. Understanding how such terms interact with the Higgs mechanism and the emergent gauge structure may shed light on the stability of gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids in realistic settings.

Third, the field theory developed here provides a natural starting point for studying dynamical probes and experimental signatures of fermionic deconfined criticality, including finite-temperature transport, dynamical structure factors, and responses to pressure or magnetic field in compounds such as SrCu2(BO3)2. More broadly, our results suggest that fermionic deconfined criticality offers a unifying paradigm for organizing quantum phase transitions and proximate spin-liquid physics across a wide class of frustrated quantum magnets, motivating its application to other lattices with reduced symmetry and complex unit cells.

Finally, from a field-theoretic perspective, several extensions of the present analysis are particularly natural. While our conclusions rely on a controlled large-NN expansion to determine operator relevance and stability, it would be valuable to complement this approach with alternative analytical techniques that are sensitive to finite-NN effects, such as conformal bootstrap methods applied to SO⁡(5)\mathrm{SO}(5)-symmetric or weakly broken fixed points, or functional renormalization-group approaches that can capture runaway flows and walking behavior beyond leading order. Such methods may help quantify the extent to which the pseudocritical regime persists at physical values of NN and clarify the nature of the eventual infrared fate.

In addition, the structure of the Majorana–Higgs theory suggests a broader landscape of nearby critical and multicritical points, including the possibility of tuning between distinct Higgs condensates or coupling multiple Higgs sectors. Exploring whether such extensions admit stable fixed points, complex fixed points, or lines of walking behavior may provide further insight into the universality and robustness of fermionic deconfined criticality. More generally, developing a systematic classification of allowed Higgs theories descending from SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) �\pi-flux states on lattices with reduced symmetry could help identify which aspects of deconfined criticality are truly universal and which depend sensitively on microscopic lattice structure.

U�x​y​(𝒓,mx,my)=(−1)�(mx,my),(B,B)​i​�y,\displaystyle U_{\sigma_{xy}}({\bm{r}},m_{x},m_{y})=(-1)^{\delta_{(m_{x},m_{y}),(B,B)}}i\tau^{y}\,,
U𝒯​(𝒓,mx,my)=−(−1)�mx,my​i​�z.\displaystyle U_{\mathcal{T}}({\bm{r}},m_{x},m_{y})=-(-1)^{\delta_{m_{x},m_{y}}}i\tau^{z}\,. (A.7)

In this gauge, the structure of the ansatz is given by Eqs. (8)–(17). Figure 9 illustrates the sign structures of the mean-field hopping and pairing amplitudes of the descendant Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} ansatz labeled by Z3000 (which is also connected to Z2Az​zzz13 on the square lattice). Notice that in the illustrated gauge form, the connection to the parent U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state U800 is explicit as the removal of the pairing terms gives the parent state.

The gaplessness of the Z3000 state is not accidental, but protected by its projective symmetry group (PSG) [66, 32]. After the parent U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state is higgsed down to Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}, the remaining projective implementation of time-reversal and Shastry–Sutherland lattice symmetries forbids any symmetry-preserving fermion bilinear mass term for the Dirac spinons [31]. Consequently, weak perturbations that preserve the full PSG can at most renormalize the Dirac velocities, shift the node positions, or generate higher-derivative corrections, but they cannot open a gap [31]. In this sense, Z3000 is a symmetry-protected gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid, in direct analogy with the square-lattice Z2Az​zzz13 state to which it is connected by PSG and adiabatic interpolation [32, 33]. More generally, this fits into the symmetry-fractionalization perspective developed for gapless Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids, where the interplay of time reversal with crystalline symmetries can forbid a fully symmetric gapped spectrum [38, 31]. Beyond mean field, the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge field is gapped, so the state is not destabilized by gauge confinement; the remaining possible instabilities are therefore associated with sufficiently strong symmetry-breaking perturbations or with a transition out of the Z3000 phase itself.

Appendix D Useful integrals

In this Appendix, we exemplify the extraction of the logarithmic divergences via dimensional regularization for some of the integrals which appear in our treatment.

D.1 Fermion self-energy

We can calculate the fermion self-energy Eq. (66) as

∫d3​q(2​�)3​q̸+k̸(k+q)2​q=12​∫01d​x​∫d3​q(2​�)3​x−1/2(q̸+k̸)[(1−x)​(k+q)2+x​q2]3/2=12​∫01d​x​∫d3​l(2​�)3​x−1/2(l̸+xk̸)[l2+x⁡(1−x)​k2]3/2=∫01d​x​12​(4​�)3/2​[x​k̸�⁡(3/2)​�⁡(0)[x⁡(1−x)​k2]0]→−16​�2​k̸​log⁡k\begin{split}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{\not{q}+\not{k}}{(k+q)^{2}q}&=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{x^{-1/2}(\not{q}+\not{k})}{[(1-x)(k+q)^{2}+xq^{2}]^{3/2}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}l}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{x^{-1/2}(\not{l}+x\not{k})}{[l^{2}+x(1-x)k^{2}]^{3/2}}\\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\frac{1}{2(4\pi)^{3/2}}\left[\frac{\sqrt{x}\not{k}}{\Gamma(3/2)}\frac{\Gamma(0)}{[x(1-x)k^{2}]^{0}}\right]\\ &\rightarrow-\frac{1}{6\pi^{2}}\not{k}\log k\end{split} (D.2)

�⁡(�)��≈1/�1+�​log⁡�≈1�−log⁡�→−log⁡k2=−2​log⁡k.\frac{\Gamma(\epsilon)}{\Delta^{\epsilon}}\approx\frac{1/\epsilon}{1+\epsilon\log\Delta}\approx\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\log\Delta\rightarrow-\log k^{2}=-2\log k\,. (D.3)

The second integral similarly gives

∫d3​q(2​�)3​q̸⁡(q̸+k̸)​q̸(k+q)2​q3=32​∫01d​x​∫d3​q(2​�)3​x​q̸​(q̸+k̸)​q̸[(1−x)​(k+q)2+x​q2]5/2=32​∫01d​x​x​∫d3​l(2​�)3​(l̸−(1−x)​k̸)​(l̸+x​k̸)​(l̸−(1−x)​k̸)[l2+x⁡(1−x)​k2]5/2→32∫01dxx​(−2​log⁡k)8​�​�⋅2​�​(5/2)��​�[−(1−x)(��k̸+k̸��)+x�k̸�]=∫01d​x​−2​x​log⁡k8​�2​[−3​(1−x)​k̸−x​k̸−3​(1−x)​k̸]=∫01d​x​−2​x​(5​x−6)8​�2​k̸​log⁡k=12​�2​k̸​log⁡k.\begin{split}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{\not{q}(\not{q}+\not{k})\not{q}}{(k+q)^{2}q^{3}}&=\frac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{\sqrt{x}\not{q}(\not{q}+\not{k})\not{q}}{[(1-x)(k+q)^{2}+xq^{2}]^{5/2}}\\ &=\frac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\sqrt{x}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}l}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{(\not{l}-(1-x)\not{k})(\not{l}+x\not{k})(\not{l}-(1-x)\not{k})}{[l^{2}+x(1-x)k^{2}]^{5/2}}\\ &\rightarrow\frac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\frac{\sqrt{x}(-2\log k)}{8\pi\sqrt{\pi}\cdot 2\Gamma(5/2)}\delta_{\mu\nu}\big[-(1-x)({}^{\mu}{}^{\nu}\not{k}+\not{k}{}^{\mu}{}^{\nu})+x{}^{\mu}\not{k}{}^{\nu}\big]\\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\frac{-2\sqrt{x}\log k}{8\pi^{2}}\big[-3(1-x)\not{k}-x\not{k}-3(1-x)\not{k}\big]\\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}x\frac{-2\sqrt{x}(5x-6)}{8\pi^{2}}\not{k}\log k\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi^{2}}\not{k}\log k\,.\end{split} (D.4)
